import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 1007

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/1007](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1007)
- [ChNo16] Chaffee, Joe and Noble, Matt, *Dimension 4 and dimension 5 graphs with minimum edge
  set*. Australas. J. Combin. (2016), 327-333.
- [Ho13] House, Roger F., *A 4-dimensional graph has at least 9 edges*. Discrete Math. (2013),
  1783-1789.
-/

namespace Erdos1007

open scoped EuclideanGeometry

variable {V : Type*}

/-- The complete tripartite graph $K_{1,3,3}$. -/
abbrev K133 := SimpleGraph.completeMultipartiteGraph fun i : Fin 3 => Fin (![1, 3, 3] i)

/--
The dimension of a graph $G$ is the minimal $n$ such that $G$ can be embedded in $\mathbb{R}^n$
such that every edge of $G$ is a unit line segment.

What is the smallest number of edges in a graph with dimension $4$?

Answer: The smallest number of edges is $9$, achieved solely by $K_{3,3}$, proved by House [Ho13]. An
alternative proof was given by Chaffee and Noble [ChNo16], who also prove that the smallest
number of edges in a graph of dimension $5$ is $15$ (achieved by $K_6$ and $K_{1,3,3}$).
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 52, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos1007.lean"]
theorem erdos_1007 :
    IsLeast {m | ∃ (n : ℕ) (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)), G.HasDimension 4 ∧ G.edgeSet.ncard = m}
      9 := by
  sorry

/--
The smallest number of edges in a graph of dimension $4$ is achieved solely by $K_{3,3}$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 52]
theorem erdos_1007.variants.dimension_four_extremal (n : ℕ) (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n))
    (hdim : G.HasDimension 4) (hcard : G.edgeSet.ncard = 9)
    (hdeg : ∀ v : Fin n, ∃ w : Fin n, G.Adj v w) :
    Nonempty (G ≃g completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 3) (Fin 3)) := by
  sorry

/--
The smallest number of edges in a graph of dimension $5$ is $15$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 52]
theorem erdos_1007.variants.dimension_five :
    IsLeast {m | ∃ (n : ℕ) (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)), G.HasDimension 5 ∧ G.edgeSet.ncard = m}
      15 := by
  sorry

/--
The smallest number of edges in a graph of dimension $5$ is achieved by $K_6$ and $K_{1,3,3}$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 52]
theorem erdos_1007.variants.dimension_five_extremal :
    ((SimpleGraph.completeGraph (Fin 6)).HasDimension 5 ∧
        (SimpleGraph.completeGraph (Fin 6)).edgeSet.ncard = 15) ∧
      (K133.HasDimension 5 ∧ K133.edgeSet.ncard = 15) := by
  sorry

end Erdos1007

reformulations.difference: The source ranges over finite simple graphs; Lean ranges over graphs whose vertex type is Fin n.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Every finite vertex type is equivalent to Fin of its cardinality. Transport along this equivalence preserves injective unit-distance representations, hence HasDimension, and induces a bijection on unordered edge sets. Therefore the sets of attainable edge counts, and their least elements, are identical. Review1007.minimum_relabeling_iff in the scratch file proves this equivalence for arbitrary dimension and proposed minimum.

reformulations.difference: Lean explicitly assumes that every vertex has a neighbor when stating uniqueness of K₃,₃. The source's uniqueness wording suppresses isolated vertices; House's proof reduces to connected graphs.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For a finite graph of dimension 4 with nine edges, deleting isolated vertices preserves both the edge count and dimension. Restricting a representation gives one direction; conversely, isolated vertices can be placed at additional distinct points in any positive-dimensional representation of the non-isolated core. The core contains edges, so dimension zero is irrelevant. Thus uniqueness among graphs without isolated vertices is equivalent to saying that every extremal graph has non-isolated core isomorphic to K₃,₃. Without this normalization, adjoining isolated vertices would defeat literal uniqueness.

reformulations.difference: As in the main theorem, arbitrary finite simple graphs are represented using vertex types Fin n.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The same finite-relabeling equivalence preserves dimension and edge cardinality. The generic scratch theorem Review1007.minimum_relabeling_iff applies with dimension 5 and minimum 15.

review.notes: Checked K133 and all four theorems. The dimension definition correctly requires distinct vertex images and unit lengths only for edges; it does not require an induced representation. Lean computations confirmed that K133 has seven vertices and fifteen edges, K6 has fifteen edges, and K3,3 has nine edges. Boundary tests establish dimension zero for empty/singleton vertex types; finite edge sets avoid ncard's infinite-set default. The source supports every research-solved tag. The dimension-five extremal variant states attainment by the two named graphs, matching the problem page; it does not claim the paper's stronger exhaustive classification. The linked formal proof has matching definitions and conclusion and no sorry/custom axioms in its text. Its certificate was not revalidated under its specified Lean/Mathlib 4.29.1 toolchain: an attempted compilation with the supplied 4.33.1 environment produced compatibility errors. This is not evidence of a statement or status defect. Successful statement tests and equivalence proofs are in /workspace/review/scratch.lean; the named equivalence proofs have no sorryAx dependency.
